https://www.businesstoday.in/world/story.text: Europe is entering a new phase of security anxiety. Governments are not saying a major war with Russia is imminent, but warnings from senior leaders, suspected drone and sabotage incidents and a growing push to prepare civilians and critical infrastructure show that European capitals are planning for a more dangerous security environment. The latest warning came from French President Emmanuel Macron on September 18. After briefing political party leaders at the Élysée Palace, Macron said the Russian hybrid threat facing France and Europe had intensified in recent weeks. He ordered preparations for a plan to protect critical infrastructure and sensitive defence-industry and technology sites from drone and cyberattacks. Macron also issued a stark warning: Europe should not expect advance notice if Russia moves from hybrid operations to a physical attack. Macron: Europe will not be warned Macron's comments followed a French Defence and National Security Council meeting on September 16 and a series of suspicious incidents across Europe. He referred to an August incident at Leipzig in Germany, where an explosive-laden drone was reportedly involved in an operation attributed to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU. Macron said the operation failed but could have caused significant casualties and material damage. He also pointed to drone incursions into the airspace of several European countries, arguing that their geographical reach showed that "no one is safe". His warning was direct: Europe has already faced information operations, cyberattacks and physical incidents attributed to Russia, but these attacks did not come with warnings. "The day we are attacked physically, we will not be warned," Macron said, arguing that Europe must raise its vigilance now. Macron, however, framed the immediate challenge as a hybrid threat, rather than announcing that Europe was heading into conventional war. Why European leaders are worried The concern extends beyond the battlefield in Ukraine. European officials are increasingly worried that Russia could test NATO's resolve through drone or missile attacks on alliance territory as Moscow expands its campaign of hybrid operations across Europe. For years, European governments largely treated Russian cyberattacks, disinformation, espionage and sabotage as threats below the threshold of conventional warfare. Recent incidents are forcing officials to consider what could happen if such operations become more aggressive or cause significant civilian casualties. That is particularly sensitive for NATO. A deliberate armed attack on a member could trigger consultations under Article 5, although the treaty does not prescribe an automatic military response in every circumstance. This uncertainty is one reason European governments are placing greater emphasis on deterrence and preparedness. Incidents behind the alarm The recent concerns go beyond drones. France has reported a series of suspicious incidents, while other European countries have investigated suspected sabotage and cyber operations. Reports have cited incidents including the Leipzig drone operation, railway disruptions in the Netherlands and a September 11 train derailment between Caen and Rouen after a large section of rail was placed across the tracks, injuring 44 people. French authorities have also investigated fires near the Eurenco explosives facility in Sorgues. European governments have been careful to distinguish between suspicion and established attribution. Not every unexplained incident has been publicly linked to Russia. The term "hybrid warfare" itself covers a broad range of activities, including cyberattacks, sabotage, influence operations and disinformation, alongside other methods intended to disrupt or intimidate an adversary. UK has been preparing civilians Britain has taken preparedness beyond military planning. The UK government has encouraged households to maintain basic emergency supplies, including food, water, first-aid materials, torches and ways to receive information during major disruptions. Officials have stressed that the advice is not simply about preparing for war. It also covers cyberattacks, power outages, flooding, infrastructure failures and other emergencies. But the timing is significant. The UK's 2026 public preparedness survey found that 28% of respondents considered it likely or very likely that war could affect their local area within two years. The survey also examined whether households had basic emergency supplies. Britain is simultaneously increasing military preparedness. The government has announced a £15 billion funding boost for the armed forces, including more than £5 billion for drones, £790 million for protection against air, drone and missile threats, and £11 billion to increase weapons and munitions stockpiles. That combination — civilian resilience and military investment — is increasingly visible across Europe. France prepares for drones, cyberattacks & sabotage Macron has instructed the French government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure and the most sensitive sites in the country's defence industrial and technological base. France is also strengthening its response to foreign interference and cyberattacks. Macron pointed to institutions such as VIGINUM, which monitors foreign interference, and legislation covering foreign interference and cyber threats. The concern is not limited to military bases. Critical infrastructure includes energy, communications, transport, technology and other systems whose disruption could affect daily life and national security. A successful attack on such infrastructure could cause significant disruption without a conventional military assault. Is Russia preparing to attack NATO? This is where the distinction between risk and expectation matters. European leaders are preparing for the possibility that Russia could expand its hybrid operations and potentially test NATO territory. But that does not mean European governments have announced that Russia is preparing an imminent conventional invasion of NATO. Macron said Russia had multiplied attacks against European interests since the summer and argued that the nature of Russian aggression in Europe was changing. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also warned about the possibility of Russian drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine. Macron described Tusk's warning as serious and said Europe should not underestimate incidents such as Leipzig. Ukraine remains central Macron has explicitly linked Europe's security concerns to continued support for Ukraine. His argument is that Russia's campaign is also intended to intimidate European governments and weaken their willingness to support Kyiv. France therefore intends to continue supporting Ukraine while strengthening its own defences against hybrid attacks. This leaves Europe facing a difficult calculation: supporting Ukraine carries security and economic risks, but European leaders increasingly view the outcome of the war as directly connected to the continent's long-term security.

https://business-review.eu/business/heal.text: UpMedical: True aesthetic confidence only happens when the body is in balance from within A new clinic reinforces a shift already underway in the local medical market: the boundaries between dermatology, aesthetics, and internal medicine are becoming increasingly difficult to define. UpMedical Primăverii—the latest addition to the UpMedical network—is built on the premise that a patient cannot be treated “in pieces,” and that the future of the industry lies in integration rather than isolated specialization. BR spoke with Dr. Cătălina Moinescu & Dr. Valentin Moinescu, founders of UpMedical, and found out more about the business and its evolution. By Romanita Oprea When you first launched UpMedical, what were your main goals? Dr. Valentin Moinescu: When we laid the foundation of UpMedical, our goal was simple: to restore coherence and humanity to a healthcare journey that had become deeply fragmented. In standard private care, patients often find themselves navigating a revolving door of isolated appointments—spending few minutes with one doctor, only to be handed an offhand referral to another, leaving them to connect the dots of their own health. Our vision with our first hub in Domenii was to build a sanctuary of multidisciplinary continuity. We wanted patients to walk into a clinic where their medical narrative remains intact across every specialty—from cardiology and internal medicine to endocrinology and dermatology. It was about creating an ecosystem where a patient never feels like a file or a transaction, but a human being whose time, anxieties, and clinical history are met with thorough diagnostic rigor, accessible ultrasound imaging, and genuine collaboration among specialists under one roof. Our patients consistently value that we don’t watch the clock—every consultation lasts as long as needed to address all of their questions. Dr. Cătălina Moinescu: Our evolution wasn’t dictated by market opportunism; it was guided by listening closely to our patients in the consultation room. Over time, we noticed a recurring pattern: so many concerns that initially presented as purely aesthetic questions—stubborn adult acne, sudden hair thinning, persistent skin dullness, unexplained weight changes, or the complex shifts of perimenopause—had deep, overlooked metabolic and hormonal roots. Treating those issues with a superficial cream or a quick filler felt like a disservice to the patient. It became clear that aesthetic medicine cannot exist in a vacuum; it must be firmly rooted in internal medicine. Our philosophy evolved into the concept of the “Whole Patient” —an integrative vision where we stop merely masking symptoms on the surface and instead investigate the underlying biological mechanisms. We realized that true aesthetic confidence only happens when the body is in balance from within. Today we expand our services to 16 medical specialties, most of them reimbursed by National Insurance House, including medical analysis, covering both medical and surgical specialties, aesthetic and longevity, with more than 35 doctors. You decided to expand and launch a second location in the Primăverii neighbourhood. How did you choose the location? Dr. Cătălina Moinescu: We chose Primăverii Plaza deliberately because location is not merely an address; it sets the emotional tone for the care experience. Many clinics choose street-level storefronts with high foot traffic, but our patients value discretion, privacy, and calm. Located on the 5th floor at Bulevardul Primăverii 19–21, the clinic acts as an intimate haven away from the city’s noise. We wanted an environment where a patient can step out of an intense executive schedule or family commitments and enter a quiet, elegant space where they feel instantly unhurried and protected. Primăverii offered the exact balance of refined accessibility and understated discretion that allows patients to arrive, undergo sensitive consultations or treatments, and leave without feeling exposed. What are the main differences compared to the Domenii clinic? Dr. Valentin Moinescu: The two clinics are designed to complement each other, serving distinct stages of a patient’s wellness continuum. UpMedical Domenii is our comprehensive clinical engine. It is a broad, multidisciplinary center housing over fifteen clinical specialties, extensive ultrasound diagnostics, and preventative consultations—operating with both private appointments and National Health Insurance (CAS) contracts to ensure wide community access. UpMedical Primăverii, is a boutique medical center, dedicated to both Medicine and Regenerative Aesthetics. It ensures a private and intentionally quiet location, focusing on the synergy between advanced medical aesthetics, plastic surgery, dermatology, and restorative hormonal and metabolic care. While Domenii delivers the wide diagnostic net that protects overall health, Primăverii translates that internal health into visible vitality, tailored tissue regeneration, and refined personal confidence. How are you positioning in the market, and what are the people you are targeting? Dr. Cătălina Moinescu: Our positioning bridges a critical gap in the private healthcare sector: we are built specifically for patients who want both comprehensive, interdisciplinary medical services—including laboratory analyses and diagnostic imaging—and advanced aesthetic treatments, all integrated within a unified care pathway. For too long, patients have been forced to navigate two entirely separate worlds. On one side, traditional medical polyclinics handle pathology, blood panels, and chronic issues, but treat aesthetic concerns as an afterthought. On the other side, high-street aesthetic clinics deliver injectables and device treatments in complete isolation from the patient’s internal health, often overlooking root causes like endocrine imbalances, vitamin deficiencies, or metabolic shifts. We deliberately position ourselves at the intersection of both. Our target patients are individuals who understand that you cannot truly decouple outward appearance from internal physiology. They are patients dealing with concerns such as adult acne, hair thinning, skin laxity, or changes during perimenopause, who do not want a superficial quick fix. Instead, they want to sit down with a medical team that will review their blood tests, coordinate between dermatology, endocrinology, and internal medicine, and then craft a safe, advanced aesthetic plan. Ultimately, we serve people who value both clinical precision and aesthetic excellence—patients who expect medical rigor behind every beauty decision, and aesthetic refinement backed by solid medical diagnostics. What are your most important services? Dr. Cătălina Moinescu: Every service we offer is designed to support the body’s innate biological structure rather than impose artificial volume: Biostimulation & Tissue Regeneration: Treatments like poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra) and high-concentration hyaluronic acid bioremodeling (Profhilo) that awaken the body’s fibroblasts to produce its own collagen and elastin over time. Integrated Clinical Specialties: Coordinated consultations in dermatology, endocrinology, gynecology, plastic surgery, and internal medicine, ensuring that issues like hormonal breakouts or hair loss are investigated from the inside out. Precision Medical Aesthetics: Conservative, anatomical wrinkle reduction and natural facial rebalancing, alongside advanced microneedling and tailored growth-factor therapies. Advanced Non-Invasive Technologies: Triple-wave laser hair removal and non-invasive body contouring designed for clinical safety and maximum patient comfort. What about the ones that differentiate you from your competition? Dr. Cătălina Moinescu: Our greatest differentiator is our clinical threshold: in our clinic, the procedure is never the starting point. 1. Mandatory Diagnostic Evaluation: We never sell off-the-shelf treatments. If someone walks in requesting an injectable that isn’t medically indicated or would compromise their natural features, our doctors have the ethical integrity to say “no” and explain why. 2. Signature Protocols like Smart Slim: Instead of treating body contouring as a standalone device session, we integrate it with metabolic screening, endocrinological guidance, and medical lifestyle support. The aesthetic device supports the journey, but the internal health changes sustain the results. Cross-Desk Collaboration: If a patient comes in for thinning hair, our dermatologist doesn’t work in isolation—they can consult directly with our in-house endocrinologist to review thyroid markers and ferritin levels within the same team. That interdisciplinary dialogue saves our patients months of guesswork. What are your business goals for the first year? Dr. Valentin Moinescu: For this first year in Primăverii, our primary objective is not rapid volume—it is establishing an uncompromising benchmark for clinical trust and patient retention. Specifically, our goals center on: · Validating the Integrative Care Model: Demonstrating that patients respond with immense loyalty when treated with medical honesty, extended consultation times, and natural regenerative results rather than high-pressure sales. · Creating Seamless Patient Pathways: Establishing a smooth, bidirectional referral bridge between our Domenii clinical hub and the Primăverii aesthetic boutique, ensuring continuity of care. · Measuring Patient Outcomes & Satisfaction: Cementing our reputation through long-term patient satisfaction, low complication rates, and word-of-mouth trust across Bucharest’s executive and family communities. When a patient leaves UpMedical feeling seen, understood, and confident that their health is in caring, capable hands, business growth follows natural.
